title: IQP Inspections for Access-Controlled Doors: The Compliance Check Most NZ Building Owners Overlook
description: Every access-controlled door in a New Zealand building with a compliance schedule carries a legal obligation under the Building Act — an annual inspection by an Independently Qualified Person, or IQP. The door must be inspected, tested, and reported to the local council each year, confirming it is performing to its specified standard. In practice, most building owners either do not know this applies to them, or they leave it until a compliance failure surfaces during a council audit. Red Wolf holds IQP qualifications and carries out these inspections as part of a broader access control service. We check that each door is latching, locking, and releasing correctly under all conditions — including alarm activation and power failure. If it is not performing to standard, we fix it and issue the required documentation. With the end of the calendar year approaching, now is a practical time to check whether your compliance schedule is current. If you are not sure whether your doors need an inspection, we can tell you in a short conversation what is required and what it will cost.

title: A New Study Found That Less Than Half of Organisations Are Confident in Their Active Assailant Response — Here Is What NZ Businesses Should Do About It
description: ASIS International and Everbridge released research this week showing that less than half of respondents are highly or mostly confident their staff know what to do in an active assailant incident. Four factors were linked to higher confidence: a comprehensive written plan, regular drills, communications technology, and a functioning behavioural threat assessment and management team. The gap between having a security system and having a prepared organisation is exactly what this finding describes. A camera at the front door and a monitored alarm panel do not tell your staff what to do when something happens. Physical security has two components — the technology layer and the human layer. Most businesses invest in the first and largely ignore the second. The organisations with the highest confidence in their readiness have both: documented procedures, tested regularly, supported by the right technology, and owned by someone with the authority to act. If your business has never run a scenario exercise or reviewed its emergency response documentation, that gap is worth closing before you need it.

title: 91% of Customer-Facing Workers Faced Aggression: What NZ Retail Should Change
description:
The NZSA signed the ShopCare Retail Pledge last week, formally recognising occupational violence and aggression as a critical risk in retail. The pledge follows the ShopCare National Customer Aggression Survey, which found 91% of customer-facing workers experienced customer aggression in the past year.

That figure changes what physical security means on a retail floor. The main threat is no longer just the after-hours break-in. It is the confrontation at the counter at 3pm. In the same week, ASIS International released its revised, ANSI-approved Workplace Violence Prevention and Intervention Standard. The standard is built around evaluating current programmes, assigning clear roles and committing to continuous improvement. For NZ retailers and hospitality operators, the practical response combines people and systems. That means duress buttons that reach a monitored response and CCTV positioned to capture faces at points of sale. It also means controlled back-of-house doors that give staff a safe retreat, and clear procedures for when to step back rather than intervene. Technology does not replace training, but it shortens the time between an incident starting and help arriving.

If your Auckland or Wellington store team is dealing with aggression, we can help you find where your current setup leaves staff exposed. Send us a message to book a site review.

title: Why Johnson Controls Wants Zero Trust Around Your Building Control Systems
description:
Johnson Controls released a white paper last week on AI-augmented attacks against operational technology. It cites the thousands of zero-day vulnerabilities found this year as evidence the threat is real, and its answer is a zero-trust overlay for OT systems.

For NZ building owners this is not abstract. Access control, CCTV, intruder alarms and building management systems now sit on networks. Many were installed years ago with flat architectures and default trust between devices. As a Johnson Controls partner, Red Wolf brings enterprise-grade capability to Wellington and Auckland sites where security systems and building controls share infrastructure. In practice, we segment security devices from corporate and BMS traffic and enforce authenticated device-to-server communication. We also remove unused services and make firmware patching part of scheduled maintenance rather than an afterthought. Most importantly, we design so that a compromised camera or controller cannot become a path into the rest of the building. The partnership gives us access to the engineering thinking behind this approach, along with the responsibility to apply it properly on NZ sites.

When choosing a security provider, ask how they protect the systems they install, not just what those systems protect. Send us a message to talk through your building's OT exposure.

title: What Procurement Teams Should Ask a Security Provider Before Shortlisting
description:

Our approach is to put the evidence up front rather than wait for clarification questions. That starts with NZSA membership and the professional standards it carries. title: Before the Christmas Shutdown: Which Security Gap Will You Close?
description:
Last week we published our poll results on the biggest physical security gap in NZ businesses. Our takeaway was blunt: you can't fix the gaps you haven't found.

With Christmas less than two months away, now is the window to act on that before Wellington and Auckland businesses wind down for summer. The holiday period is when sites sit empty longest, staff rotate out, and faults go unnoticed until January. It is also when budgets for the new year are being shaped. A year-end security review doesn't need to be large. Check who still holds active access credentials, and confirm alarm and monitoring contacts are current over the break. Test duress and intercom points, and list any devices that failed or needed patching this year. Red Wolf's position is that the most useful review ends with a short, prioritised list, not a long report that sits in a drawer. Three fixes done in December beat thirty recommendations left for next year.

So we want to hear it: what is the one security gap your organisation wants closed before the year ends? Drop a comment below, and we'll share the common themes in a follow-up post.
